pull.title: BIP395: Unspendable Internal Keys for Wallet Policies
pull.body:
This proposes `_` as an unspendable Taproot internal-key placeholder in wallet policies. Wallets and signers can reproduce the internal key from the policy and derivation path, without keeping a separate random tweak.

The construction uses the BIP 341 NUMS point as the public key of a synthetic BIP 32 root. Its chain code commits to the normalized policy, including both the keys and the policy structure. Child keys are then derived using unhardened BIP 32 derivation.

This builds on the [Delving discussion](https://delvingbitcoin.org/t/unspendable-keys-in-descriptors/304) and the earlier work in #1746. I shared an earlier draft on the [Bitcoin Development Mailing List](https://groups.google.com/g/bitcoindev/c/se3TkNnbno4).

I've included a Python reference implementation, fixed JSON test vectors, and instructions for running the checks. All 21 offline tests pass, and the export and derivation cross-check passes all 20 cases against Bitcoin Core 31.0.

Perhaps worth a line on the post-quantum verification property described in https://groups.google.com/g/bitcoindev/c/se3TkNnbno4/m/NC5TeBFrBAAJ (anyone with the policy can re-derive the internal key and prove the key path was unspendable).

```diff
A Taproot policy that uses a fixed unspendable internal key produces outputs that are recognizable when script-path spends reveal that key. [[bip-0341.mediawiki#constructing-and-spending-taproot-outputs|BIP 341]] recommends ''H + rG'' with a fresh ''r''. Current implementations use various approaches, such as taking entropy from the keys or choosing and retaining a random ''r''. Deriving the public tweaks from a policy commitment lets independent implementations reproduce the internal key from a policy backup, without additional secret material. Committing to the policy's structure also distinguishes descriptors that use the same keys under different spending conditions.
+
+Anyone holding the policy can also re-derive the internal key and thereby prove the key path was unspendable. This can be useful in post-quantum settings or for exposure classification.
```

> Including them in the commitment would give an xpub and its tpub form, or the same key with and without an origin, different internal keys for identical addresses.

This sentence is correct, but a bit hard to parse, I would restructure it as:

> Including them in the commitment would produce different internal keys for an xpub and its tpub form, or for the same key with and without an origin, even though these generate identical scripts.

Also I would say identical scripts rather than identical addresses, because in the xpub vs tpub form the address would change, because of different network bytes (e.g. `bc1`... vs `tb1`...)
